plan: Ten new items. Every topic and word checked against the live SAT R&W bank after the 300-item audit (dropped 'ephemeral' (in 251) and a 'corroborated' item that repeated 105's 'borne out' concept). makeshift/prescient WIC, slime-mold structure, moai inference, phone reaction-time data (two-part-looking distractors), elephant seismic-hypothesis evidence, Hedy Lamarr purpose synthesis, 'That said,' exception transition, semicolon series, subjunctive after 'required that' (a 'the number of' item was dropped because the screen matched it to 067). Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: S035-02 medium→easy, S035-03 medium→easy, S035-04 hard→medium, S035-06 hard→easy, S035-07 medium→easy, S035-10 hard→medium.

passages.title: A field clinic
passages.text: After the flood cut the town's only road, volunteers set up a ______ clinic in the school gym: folding tables served as examination beds, bedsheets hung from volleyball nets divided the patients, and car batteries powered the lamps.

passages.title: An early warning
passages.text: In 1896, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling the carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere would warm the planet by several degrees. Most of his contemporaries thought the effect too small or too distant to matter, but measurements taken more than a century later suggest that his basic conclusion was ______.

passages.title: A brainless network
passages.text: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum is a single cell with no brain or nervous system. In one experiment, researchers placed oat flakes, a food the mold seeks out, on a dish in a pattern matching the locations of cities around Tokyo. The mold first spread across the dish and then pulled back, leaving a network of tubes connecting the food sources that closely resembled the region's actual rail system. Engineers have since studied how the mold builds such networks for ideas about designing efficient transportation and communication systems.

passages.title: Walking statues
passages.text: The moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) are stone statues, many weighing several tons, that were moved long distances from the quarry where they were carved. Because the island had few large trees when Europeans arrived, some researchers doubted that the statues could have been dragged lying down on wooden sledges, which would have required large amounts of timber. Island oral traditions say that the moai "walked" to their platforms. In 2012, researchers tied ropes to the head of an upright concrete replica and, by rocking it from side to side, moved it about 100 meters in under an hour with a team of 18 people. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Phones and braking
passages.text:
In a driving-simulator study, researchers measured how long participants took to brake after a car ahead of them stopped suddenly.
Condition | Average reaction time (seconds)
No phone call | 0.9
Hands-free phone call | 1.3
Handheld phone call | 1.4
The researchers concluded that hands-free calls slow drivers' reactions nearly as much as handheld calls do.

passages.title: Listening with their feet
passages.text: Elephants produce low rumbling calls, and the vibrations from these calls travel through the ground as well as through the air. Biologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell hypothesized that elephants can detect such ground vibrations and respond to them.

passages.title: Hedy Lamarr's invention
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hedy Lamarr was a film actress who also worked on inventions.
• In 1942, she and the composer George Antheil received a patent for a "secret communication system."
• The system rapidly switched a radio signal among 88 frequencies.
• Its purpose was to keep enemies from jamming the radio signals used to guide torpedoes.
• The number 88 matched the number of keys on a piano.

passages.title: Rocks from Mars
passages.text: Most meteorites found on Earth are fragments of asteroids. ______ a small number come from Mars: gases trapped inside them closely match the Martian atmosphere as measured by the Viking landers in 1976.

passages.title: A three-port voyage
passages.text: On its first voyage, the steamship called at three ports along the Pacific coast of South America: Valparaíso, Chile; Callao, Peru______ Guayaquil, Ecuador.

passages.title: A ferry safety rule
passages.text: After an inspection found that several life jackets on the island ferry had been stored behind locked panels, the harbor authority required that every vessel ______ its safety equipment where passengers can reach it without tools.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: folding tables served as examination beds
candidates.explanation: Everyday objects pressed into service as beds, walls, and power describe a clinic put together from whatever was available: "makeshift."

A.rationale: Folding tables and hanging bedsheets describe a temporary setup, not a permanent one.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the clinic treated one kind of patient or used special equipment.

D.rationale: Folding tables and bedsheets are the opposite of luxurious.

hints: What were the beds and walls made of?

strategy.explanation: Predict "thrown together from whatever was on hand."

candidates.remember: Use the details after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: measurements taken more than a century later suggest
candidates.explanation: A conclusion doubted at the time but supported a century later showed foresight: it was "prescient."

B.rationale: His figure came from calculation, and later measurements supported it, so it was not arbitrary.

C.rationale: Later measurements supported his conclusion rather than replacing it.

D.rationale: Whether the conclusion was deliberate is not the point; the text contrasts his contemporaries' doubts with later support.

hints: What did later measurements show about his conclusion?
candidates.remember: Contrast words like "but" signal that the blank reverses the earlier view.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a theory about how rail systems are designed and then rejects it using evidence from an experiment.
choices.B: It compares two organisms' abilities and then explains which one engineers prefer to study.
choices.C: It describes a problem with Tokyo's rail system and then proposes a solution based on biology.
choices.D: It describes a surprising result involving a simple organism and then explains why the result interests engineers.

candidates.evidence: Engineers have since studied how the mold builds such networks
candidates.explanation: The text describes the mold, the Tokyo experiment and its rail-like result, and ends with engineers' interest in the mold's network-building.

A.rationale: No theory about rail design is presented or rejected.

C.rationale: No problem with the rail system is described.

hints: What does the last sentence add?
candidates.remember: Structure questions ask how the parts of a text fit together.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the moai were carved at the platforms where they now stand rather than at a distant quarry.
choices.B: the islanders may have moved the moai upright, using ropes rather than large amounts of timber.
choices.C: the island's oral traditions about the moai are unrelated to how the statues were actually moved.
choices.D: the islanders must have cut down all of the island's trees to build sledges for the moai.

candidates.evidence: by rocking it from side to side, moved it about 100 meters
candidates.explanation: The doubts about sledges, the "walking" traditions, and the successful rocking test all point to the statues being moved upright with ropes.

A.rationale: The text says the statues were moved long distances from the quarry.

C.rationale: The replica test matches the traditions' description of the statues "walking."

D.rationale: The experiment points away from sledges; nothing shows the trees were cut for this purpose.

hints: What method does the experiment demonstrate?

strategy.explanation: Combine the three pieces of evidence before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: "Taken together" means the answer must fit every piece of evidence given.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Compared with no call, a hands-free call raised the average by 0.4 second and a handheld call raised it by 0.5 second.
choices.B: The average was 0.9 seconds with no call, 0.4 second less than the 1.3 seconds with a hands-free call.
choices.C: The average was 0.9 seconds with no call, 0.5 second less than the 1.4 seconds with a handheld call.
choices.D: The average with either kind of call was more than 1.2 seconds, while with no call it was under 1 second.

candidates.evidence: hands-free calls slow drivers' reactions nearly as much as handheld calls do
candidates.explanation: The conclusion is about how much each kind of call slows reactions. Measured from the 0.9-second baseline, hands-free calls add 0.4 second and handheld calls 0.5 second, so the hands-free slowdown is nearly as large.

B.rationale: This shows hands-free calls slow reactions but does not compare them with handheld calls.

C.rationale: This compares no call with handheld calls and leaves out hands-free calls.

D.rationale: This shows both kinds of calls slow reactions but does not compare how much each one slows them.

hints: How much does each kind of call slow reactions?

strategy.explanation: Measure each slowdown from the no-call baseline.

candidates.remember: Match the claim's comparison to the data, not just any true comparison.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support O'Connell-Rodwell's hypothesis?

choices.A: When warning calls were played through loudspeakers in the air, elephants at a water hole gathered together and became more alert.
choices.B: Recordings made at several water holes showed that elephants' rumbling calls include frequencies far too low for human ears to hear.
choices.C: When warning calls were played only as vibrations through the ground, with no sound in the air, elephants at a water hole gathered together and became more alert.
choices.D: Elephants visiting the water hole produced rumbling calls more often at dusk than at any other time of day, especially in the dry season.

candidates.evidence: elephants can detect such ground vibrations and respond to them
candidates.explanation: To support the hypothesis, a finding must isolate ground vibrations and show a response; only C removes airborne sound and still finds a reaction.

A.rationale: Sound traveled through the air, so this does not show that the elephants detected ground vibrations.

B.rationale: This concerns the calls themselves, not whether elephants detect them through the ground.

D.rationale: When elephants call says nothing about whether they detect ground vibrations.

hints: What must the finding rule out?

strategy.explanation: Identify exactly what the hypothesis claims.

candidates.remember: The best support isolates the factor the hypothesis is about.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain the purpose of Lamarr and Antheil's invention. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Lamarr and Antheil's 1942 system switched a radio signal among 88 frequencies, the number of keys on a piano.
choices.B: Lamarr and Antheil designed their system to keep enemies from jamming the radio signals that guided torpedoes.
choices.C: In 1942, actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil received a patent for a secret communication system.
choices.D: Hedy Lamarr, a film actress, also worked on inventions, including one patented with George Antheil in 1942.

candidates.evidence: Its purpose was to keep enemies from jamming
candidates.explanation: Only B states what the system was for: preventing enemies from jamming torpedo-guidance signals.

A.rationale: This describes how the system worked and a detail about it, not its purpose.

C.rationale: This identifies the inventors and the patent but not the purpose.

D.rationale: This describes Lamarr's career, not the invention's purpose.

strategy.explanation: Find the note that matches the goal.

candidates.remember: In synthesis questions, the goal decides the answer.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Most meteorites found on Earth are fragments of asteroids.
candidates.explanation: The first sentence states the general pattern; the second gives an exception. "That said" introduces a qualification of what came before.

A.rationale: Mars meteorites are not a result of most meteorites coming from asteroids.

B.rationale: Meteorites from Mars are not an example of fragments of asteroids.

C.rationale: Coming from Mars is an exception to the asteroid pattern, not similar to it.

hints: Is the Mars group like the general pattern or an exception to it?

strategy.explanation: Predict the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: "Most ... " followed by a smaller group signals an exception.

candidates.subskill: Semicolons in a series with internal commas
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Because each item contains a comma, items in this series are separated by semicolons; the last item follows "; and."

A.rationale: The items contain commas (city, country), so they must be separated by semicolons, as the first two already are.

C.rationale: The items must be separated by a semicolon to match the rest of the series.

D.rationale: A colon has already introduced the list and cannot separate its items.

hints: How are the first two items separated?

strategy.explanation: Match the punctuation already used in the series.

candidates.remember: When list items contain commas, separate them with semicolons.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the harbor authority required that every vessel
candidates.explanation: Verbs of requiring or demanding followed by "that" take the base form of the verb: "required that every vessel store...."

A.rationale: After "required that," standard English uses the base form of the verb (the subjunctive), not "stores."

B.rationale: The subjunctive after "required that" uses the base form, not the past tense.

D.rationale: "Storing" leaves the clause without a finite verb.

strategy.explanation: Test each form after "required that every vessel."

candidates.remember: After require, insist, recommend + that, use the base verb: "that she go."

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves matched all keys; both rated S035-05 medium because the key compared hands-free with handheld times without the no-call baseline, making distractor D (both calls above 1.2 s, no call under 1 s) a strong pull. Rewrote the key to compare the slowdowns themselves (0.4 s vs 0.5 s from the 0.9 s baseline) and adjusted D's rationale. Whole batch re-solved blind.
